title: This one pleases me (Genesis Rabbah 3:7)
hook: God built worlds and unmade them, then said of this one: it pleases me
tomorrow: before people were made, who in heaven voted no?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the torah was the blueprint. God looked into the plan, then built. Which makes today's odd little detail even odder.

Every group project has a folder of abandoned drafts: version one, version two, final, final-final. Here's a line that sounds like it came out of that folder. In Genesis, before there's any sun, the text says: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Look at the wording. Not "let there be evening." There was evening, as if evenings already had a way of happening. Some rabbis took that small phrase as a clue that this wasn't the first draft.
screen: `FINAL, FINAL-FINAL.` → `THERE WAS EVENING.` → `NOT THE FIRST DRAFT?`

segments.voice: Genesis Rabbah gives two voices. Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon says the wording shows an order of time already existed. Rabbi Abbahu goes further, and his is the line people repeat: the Holy One kept creating worlds and destroying them, until He created this one. Then He said: this one pleases Me; those did not please Me. Sit with how strange that is, a day after the blueprint. The same tradition that says God looked into a perfect plan also tells of worlds built and unbuilt. The midrash never says what was wrong with them. It doesn't describe them at all. It keeps only the verdict. And look at what the verdict isn't. It isn't "this one is perfect." This is the world with a flood and jealous brothers still ahead, the world whose own story, a few chapters on, has God regretting making people. Still: this one pleases Me. So the plan and the drafts belong together. A good plan doesn't promise the first try works. It means you know what you're building well enough to recognize it when it's in front of you, and to stop tearing down. Pleased doesn't mean finished. It means: this one, I'll keep.
screen: `THERE WAS EVENING, NOT LET THERE BE.` · `WORLDS BUILT, AND UNBUILT.` · `NOT PERFECT. CHOSEN.` · `RECOGNIZE IT, THEN KEEP IT.` · then, large: `THIS ONE PLEASES ME.`

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper and write one sentence by hand about something you care about, with no planning. Don't cross anything out. Read it once, leave it exactly as it is, and rest your eyes on it for the sit: a first draft you're allowed to keep.
This one pleases me: Rabbi Abbahu's line in Genesis Rabbah, after worlds were built and unbuilt. Not perfect. Kept.
Keep this one: this one pleases me, and a draft can be the one. See you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Rabbi Abbahu's story ends not with perfect but with a verdict: this one pleases Me. Drafts are for finding the one to keep.

Rabbi Abbahu.meaning: the sage who tells of worlds built and destroyed

sources.ref: Genesis Rabbah 3:7 (Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon on an order of time; Rabbi Abbahu: worlds built and destroyed, 'these please Me')

notes: Genesis Rabbah 3:7 paraphrased: Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon ('it is not written let there be evening') and Rabbi Abbahu ('He kept creating worlds and destroying them until He created these; He said: these please Me, those did not'). The midrash's plural 'these' (worlds) is rendered 'this one' to match the index. Confirm attribution and wording; the saying recurs in Genesis Rabbah 9:2 at 'very good'.
Puzzle shape: the odd wording 'there was evening' before the sun. Practice kind: write one line by hand.
